q: Scores of 3, 5, 5 and 8 are ranked for a non-parametric test. What ranks do they receive?
o: 1, 2, 3, 4 (no ties)
1, 2, 2, 3 (shared)
e: Tied scores share the average of the ranks they would occupy: the two 5s would take ranks 2 and 3, so each gets 2.5. The next score keeps rank 4, so the ranks still sum to n(n + 1)/2 = 10.
w: Tied scores must share a rank; giving them 2 and 3 treats equal scores as different.
Giving both 5s rank 2 and the 8 rank 3 makes the ranks sum to 8 instead of 10.
Giving both 5s the upper rank 3 makes the ranks sum to 11 instead of 10.
k: Tied scores get the average of the ranks they occupy; ranks sum to n(n + 1)/2.
h: Ties split the ranks down the middle.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Ranking data

q: Why do rank-based tests reduce the influence of outliers?
o: Ranking keeps only the order of scores, so an extreme value is just the highest rank
Ranking deletes the highest and lowest scores before the test statistic is computed
Ranking transforms the data to a normal distribution with a mean of zero
Ranking gives outliers a weight of zero in the calculation of the statistic
e: Whether the top score is 50 or 5,000, it simply becomes rank n. The information about distance is discarded, so extreme values cannot dominate the statistic. This robustness costs some power when parametric assumptions actually hold.
w: Ranking keeps every score; it doesn't delete the highest and lowest.
Ranks are uniformly spaced integers, not a normal distribution with mean zero.
Outliers keep full weight as the top or bottom rank; they just lose their distance.
k: Ranks keep order, not distance, so extreme values can't dominate.
h: 5,000 or 50, it's still just rank n.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Why ranks

q: When parametric assumptions are fully met, a non-parametric test compared with its parametric equivalent typically has:
o: Somewhat less power, because information about the distances between scores is discarded
More power, because ranks are unaffected by the variance of the scores in each group
Identical power in every situation, because both kinds of test evaluate the same hypothesis
No power at all, because ranks cannot detect differences between groups of any size
e: Ranking discards information. When the data meet parametric assumptions, a t-test or ANOVA is a little more likely to detect a real effect. When assumptions are badly violated, especially with heavy tails or outliers, rank-based tests can be the more powerful option.
w: Ranks lose distance information, so they don't gain power when assumptions hold.
Power differs: parametric tests use more information when assumptions hold.
Rank tests do detect group differences; they're only slightly less powerful.
k: When assumptions hold, rank tests have slightly less power than parametric tests.
h: Throw away distances, lose a little power.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Power

q: Which non-parametric test compares two independent groups?
o: Mann–Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test (paired version)
Friedman's two-way ANOVA by ranks
Kruskal–Wallis H test (one-way)
e: Two independent groups: Mann–Whitney U, or equivalently Wilcoxon's rank-sum W, which gives the same p-value. Two related conditions: Wilcoxon signed-rank. Three or more independent groups: Kruskal–Wallis. Three or more related conditions: Friedman.
w: Wilcoxon signed-rank compares two related conditions, not independent groups.
Friedman's ANOVA compares three or more related conditions.
Kruskal–Wallis compares three or more independent groups.
k: Two independent groups → Mann–Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum).
h: Signed goes with the Same people; Sum goes with Separate groups.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Choosing a test

q: SPSS output for a Mann–Whitney test reports both U and Wilcoxon's W. How do they relate?
o: They are equivalent statistics and give the same z and p-value
W tests medians while U tests means, so they can disagree
U is for small samples and W is used only for large samples
W is the effect size for the test, while U is the test statistic
e: Mann–Whitney's U and Wilcoxon's rank-sum W are algebraically linked: U = W − n(n + 1)/2 for the group whose ranks were summed. They lead to the same standardized z and the same p. Report one consistently, usually U.
w: U and W test the same hypothesis and can't disagree.
Both statistics apply at any sample size.
W isn't an effect size; it's an equivalent test statistic.
k: Mann–Whitney U and Wilcoxon rank-sum W are equivalent and give the same z and p.
h: U and W: two names, one test.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Mann–Whitney and Wilcoxon rank-sum

q: A Mann–Whitney test gives z = −2.80 with a total sample of N = 40. What is the effect size r?
e: r = z / √N = −2.80 / √40 = −2.80 / 6.32 = −0.44, a medium-to-large effect. N is the total number of observations. The sign only reflects which group was coded first, so interpret the size with the direction from the mean ranks.
w: −0.07 divides z by N (40) instead of √N.
−2.80 is the z itself, not converted to r.
−0.70 divides z by 4 instead of √40 ≈ 6.32.
k: Effect size for rank tests: r = z ÷ √N (total N).
h: z over root N gives r.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Effect sizes for rank tests

q: In the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which values are ranked?
o: The absolute differences between each person's two scores, ignoring zero differences
The raw scores from both conditions, pooled and ranked together across conditions
Each condition's scores separately, from lowest to highest within that condition
Only the positive differences, ranked from smallest to largest across people
e: Compute each person's difference, drop zero differences, rank the absolute values, then give each rank the sign of its difference. The test compares the sums of positive and negative ranks: if the conditions do not differ, the two sums should be similar.
w: Pooling raw scores is the Mann–Whitney approach for independent groups.
Ranking within each condition ignores the pairing.
Both positive and negative differences are ranked, then signed.
k: Wilcoxon signed-rank: rank the absolute differences, then attach their signs.
h: Rank the size, sign the direction.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Wilcoxon signed-rank test

q: The sign test differs from the Wilcoxon signed-rank test because it:
o: Uses only the direction of each difference, ignoring its size
Ranks the raw scores themselves rather than the differences between them
Requires three or more related conditions rather than just two
Assumes that the difference scores are normally distributed in the population
e: The sign test counts how many differences are positive versus negative. Wilcoxon also uses the ranks of the magnitudes, so it is usually more powerful. The sign test makes the fewest assumptions.
w: The sign test doesn't rank raw scores at all.
The sign test compares two related conditions, not three or more.
The sign test makes no normality assumption.
k: Sign test uses only the direction of differences; Wilcoxon also uses their size.
h: Sign test: just plus or minus.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Sign test

q: The Kruskal–Wallis H statistic is evaluated against which distribution?
o: Chi-square with k − 1 degrees of freedom
F with k − 1 and N − k degrees of freedom
t with N − 2 degrees of freedom
The normal distribution with mean 0 and SD 1
e: H measures how far the groups' mean ranks are from the overall mean rank, and for reasonable sample sizes it follows a χ² distribution with df = number of groups − 1. Report it as H(2) = 9.84, p = .007 for three groups.
w: F is for parametric ANOVA, not Kruskal–Wallis.
t with N − 2 df is for correlation or two groups.
The standard normal is used for two-group rank tests' z.
k: Kruskal–Wallis H ~ χ² with k − 1 df.
h: H wears a chi-square hat.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Kruskal–Wallis test

q: After a significant Kruskal–Wallis test, how does SPSS's newer non-parametric procedure handle follow-up comparisons?
o: It runs pairwise comparisons and reports Bonferroni-adjusted p-values (Adj. Sig.)
It runs Tukey's HSD on the mean ranks of the groups without any adjustment
It runs a separate one-way ANOVA on the ranks for each possible pair of groups
It provides no follow-up options, so you must run and correct pairwise t-tests manually
e: In Analyze → Nonparametric Tests → Independent Samples, pairwise comparisons appear with 'Sig.' and 'Adj. Sig.', where the adjusted value corrects for the number of comparisons. Alternatives are a planned set of Mann–Whitney tests with a corrected α, or the Jonckheere–Terpstra test for an ordered trend.
w: Tukey's HSD is a parametric post hoc test.
SPSS doesn't run ANOVAs on ranks for each pair.
SPSS does offer pairwise follow-ups in the newer procedure.
k: SPSS's newer Kruskal–Wallis gives pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni 'Adj. Sig.'.
h: Adjusted Sig. for honest pairs.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Follow-up tests

q: Groups receive 0, 1, 2 or 3 sessions of an intervention, and you predict that scores rise across these ordered groups. Which test fits this prediction best?
o: Jonckheere–Terpstra test
Kruskal–Wallis H test
Friedman's two-way ANOVA
McNemar's test
e: Kruskal–Wallis asks only whether groups differ somewhere. Jonckheere–Terpstra tests a specific ordered trend in medians across groups arranged in a meaningful order, so it has more power for that hypothesis. You must specify the order.
w: Kruskal–Wallis tests whether groups differ anywhere, not an ordered trend.
Friedman's ANOVA is for related conditions.
McNemar's test is for related binary outcomes.
k: An ordered trend across independent groups → Jonckheere–Terpstra test.
h: Jonckheere for a staircase of medians.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Jonckheere–Terpstra test

q: Each participant rated three different treatments. Which non-parametric test compares the three ratings?
o: Friedman's ANOVA
Kruskal–Wallis test
Mann–Whitney U test
Jonckheere–Terpstra test
e: Friedman's test ranks each person's scores across conditions (within each row), then compares the sum of ranks for each condition. It is the non-parametric counterpart of one-way repeated-measures ANOVA, with χ²(k − 1) as its test statistic.
w: Kruskal–Wallis is for independent groups, not the same people.
Mann–Whitney compares only two independent groups.
Jonckheere–Terpstra tests ordered trends in independent groups.
k: Three or more related conditions → Friedman's ANOVA.
h: Friedman: same friends, several conditions.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Friedman's ANOVA

q: In Friedman's ANOVA, scores are ranked:
o: Within each participant, across the conditions
Across all participants and conditions together
Within each condition, across the participants
Only for the condition with the highest median
e: Because the same people provide every score, Friedman ranks each person's scores from 1 to k. This removes individual differences, just as repeated-measures ANOVA does. Kruskal–Wallis, by contrast, ranks everyone together.
w: Ranking everyone together is the Kruskal–Wallis approach.
Ranking within each condition ignores the repeated measures.
All conditions are ranked, not just one.
k: Friedman ranks scores within each participant across conditions.
h: Rank across the row.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · How Friedman ranks

q: A Mann–Whitney test is significant. When can it be described specifically as a difference in medians?
o: When the two groups' distributions have a similar shape and spread
Whenever the test statistic U is larger than its expected value
When the sample sizes in the two groups are exactly equal
Only when both distributions are normal and have equal variances
e: Strictly, the test compares the distributions, or the probability that a score from one group exceeds a score from the other. If the shapes are similar and only the location differs, this amounts to a difference in medians. Otherwise, report differences in mean ranks or distributions.
w: U exceeding its expected value doesn't define a median difference.
Equal sample sizes don't make it a median test.
Normality and equal variances aren't required.
k: A Mann–Whitney difference is a median difference only if shapes and spreads are similar.
h: Same shape, then medians.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · What rank tests test

q: In SPSS, where are the Mann–Whitney and Kruskal–Wallis tests found in the newer interface?
o: Analyze → Nonparametric Tests → Independent Samples
Analyze → Nonparametric Tests → Related Samples
Analyze → Compare Means → Independent-Samples T Test
Analyze → General Linear Model → Univariate
e: Independent Samples covers Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis, Jonckheere–Terpstra and others, and Related Samples covers Wilcoxon, Friedman and others. You can let SPSS choose tests automatically or customize them. The older Legacy Dialogs offer the same tests with simpler output.
w: Related Samples holds Wilcoxon and Friedman tests.
Compare Means holds the parametric t-tests, not rank-based tests.
General Linear Model holds parametric ANOVA.
k: Mann–Whitney and Kruskal–Wallis: Nonparametric Tests → Independent Samples.
h: Independent groups, Independent Samples menu.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · SPSS · Non-parametric menus

q: Patients are classified as depressed or not before and after treatment. Which test assesses change in the proportion depressed?
o: McNemar's test
Pearson's chi-square test
Friedman's ANOVA
Mann–Whitney U test
e: McNemar's test handles a binary outcome measured twice on the same people. It focuses on the people who changed category (depressed → not, versus not → depressed). Pearson's χ² would wrongly treat the two measurements as independent. With three or more related binary measurements, use Cochran's Q.
w: Pearson's χ² wrongly treats the two measurements as independent.
Friedman's ANOVA is for ranked scores, not paired binary outcomes.
Mann–Whitney compares two independent groups, not the same people twice.
k: Binary outcome measured twice on the same people → McNemar's test.
h: McNemar for changers.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · McNemar's test

q: Which is an appropriate way to report a Wilcoxon signed-rank result in APA style?
e: Report the statistic (T, the smaller sum of ranks, or the value SPSS provides), the standardized z, the exact p and an effect size such as r = z / √N, plus the medians of each condition. The other options use parametric statistics or the wrong test family.
w: t and Cohen's d belong to a paired t-test.
F and partial η² belong to ANOVA.
χ² and Cramér's V belong to tests of association.
k: Report Wilcoxon as T, z, exact p and r = z/√N, plus medians.
h: T, z, p, r.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Reporting

q: A researcher has small samples, heavily skewed data with outliers, and two related conditions. The most defensible analysis is:
o: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test or a robust paired test, such as one on trimmed means
An independent t-test, because the t distribution's heavy tails already handle the skew
A Kruskal–Wallis test, because the samples are small and the data skewed
A chi-square test, after splitting the outcome variable at its median value
e: Related conditions with problematic distributions in a small sample suit the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Robust alternatives, such as a paired comparison of trimmed means or a bootstrapped CI for the mean difference, are also good options. Dichotomizing a continuous outcome throws away information.
w: An independent t-test ignores the pairing and the skew.
Kruskal–Wallis is for three or more independent groups, not related conditions.
Splitting at the median throws away information.
k: Small, skewed, related data → Wilcoxon signed-rank or a robust paired test.
h: Paired and messy: Wilcoxon or trim.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Choosing a test

q: Why can the Kruskal–Wallis test be described as a one-way ANOVA on ranks?
o: H is the between-groups sum of squares of the ranks, divided by the variance of all the ranks
It requires the same normality assumptions as ANOVA, applied to the ranks instead of the raw scores
It produces an F statistic, which SPSS simply labels as H in the output table
It compares the variances of the groups instead of comparing their central tendency
e: Replace scores with ranks and compute how far each group's mean rank lies from the overall mean rank: a between-groups sum of squares on the ranks. Dividing it by the variance of all N ranks, N(N + 1)/12, gives H, which follows χ²(k − 1). The analogy helps in remembering what the test is sensitive to.
w: Kruskal–Wallis makes no normality assumption about the ranks or scores.
SPSS reports H as a chi-square statistic, not a relabelled F.
Kruskal–Wallis compares mean ranks, not variances.
k: H = between-groups SS of ranks ÷ variance of all ranks, compared with χ².
h: ANOVA wearing rank clothes.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Kruskal–Wallis logic

q: For a Friedman or Kruskal–Wallis test, the most informative effect sizes are usually:
o: Effect sizes r = z / √N for focused pairwise comparisons
The H or χ² statistic itself, because it grows with the effect
The p-value, because smaller p-values mean larger effects
Cohen's d computed from the group medians and the range
e: Omnibus effects with several df are hard to interpret. Field recommends reporting effect sizes for specific comparisons, such as r for each follow-up test. H and χ² depend on the sample size, as does p, so neither is an effect size.
w: H and χ² grow with sample size, so they aren't effect sizes.
p depends on n, so it doesn't measure effect size.
Medians and ranges don't give a standard d.
k: Report r = z/√N for focused pairwise comparisons after omnibus rank tests.
h: Zoom in on pairs for effect sizes.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Effect sizes for omnibus tests

q: A Friedman test on four related conditions gives χ²F = 9.6. What are its degrees of freedom?
e: df = k − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3. Report it as χ²F(3) = 9.6 with the exact p (here about .02).
w: 4 uses k instead of k − 1.
9 isn't related to the number of conditions.
N − 1 would depend on participants, not conditions.
k: Friedman df = k − 1 (conditions minus 1).
h: Four conditions, three df.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Friedman degrees of freedom

q: Which pairing of a parametric test with its non-parametric counterpart is correct?
o: Paired t-test ↔ Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Independent t-test ↔ Friedman's ANOVA
One-way independent ANOVA ↔ Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Repeated-measures ANOVA ↔ Mann–Whitney U test
e: Independent t ↔ Mann–Whitney. Paired t ↔ Wilcoxon signed-rank. One-way independent ANOVA ↔ Kruskal–Wallis. One-way repeated-measures ANOVA ↔ Friedman.
w: Independent t pairs with Mann–Whitney, not Friedman.
One-way independent ANOVA pairs with Kruskal–Wallis.
Repeated-measures ANOVA pairs with Friedman's ANOVA, not Mann–Whitney.
k: Pairs: independent t–Mann–Whitney; paired t–Wilcoxon; ANOVA–Kruskal–Wallis; RM ANOVA–Friedman.
h: Mann for two groups, Wilcox for two times, Kruskal for many groups, Friedman for many times.
r: Stats & SPSS ch. 8 · Non-parametric models · Parametric counterparts
